sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Cache-aside (also called lazy loading) is a caching pattern in which the **application** explicitly manages the cache: on a read it checks the cache first, and only on a miss does it query the database and then back-fill the cache; on a write it updates the database and invalidates (or updates) the corresponding cache entry.

Cache-aside is the most common caching pattern in production because it is **simple, explicit, and gives the application full control**. The application code is the orchestrator: it knows when to read the cache, when to fall through to the database, what TTL to set, and when to invalidate. There is no magic in the cache itself — Redis or memcached is treated as a dumb key-value store, and all the policy lives in the application. Real-world: Netflix's playback service uses cache-aside with EVCache (their memcached fork) to store user profiles, language preferences, parental-control settings, and resume positions — each service reads its slice from EVCache and falls through to Cassandra only on a miss. The simplicity is the feature: engineers can reason about every read and write, and the cache never silently changes behavior under them.

The **read path** is canonical: (1) application calls `cache.get(key)`; (2) on hit, return the value immediately — sub-millisecond, no DB involvement; (3) on miss, application queries the database, then calls `cache.set(key, value, ttl)` to populate the cache for future reads, and returns the value. This is "lazy loading" — the cache is populated only when a read actually happens, so cold keys never waste cache space. Compare with read-through (next topic), where the cache itself fetches from the DB on a miss via a configured loader. Cache-aside is more verbose — every read site has the miss-handling code — but it's also more flexible: different read sites can apply different TTLs, miss-handling, or fallback strategies for the same logical key. Instagram's feed service uses cache-aside for exactly this reason — the home-feed cache has a 60-second TTL but the user-profile cache has a 1-hour TTL, and the application code controls each explicitly.

The **write path** has two variants, and the choice matters. **Update-the-cache**: on write, update the DB then `cache.set(key, new_value, ttl)`. This keeps the cache warm but introduces a race — if a concurrent read also computes the value and writes it back, last-writer-wins may leave stale data. **Invalidate-the-cache**: on write, update the DB then `cache.del(key)` so the next read misses and re-populates from the DB. This is safer because invalidation is idempotent and order-independent, but it incurs one extra miss on the next read. Most production systems use invalidation for safety. Netflix's profile service invalidates the cache key after a profile update — the next read takes a 5 ms hit (one Cassandra read) instead of the usual 0.5 ms cache hit, but the data is guaranteed fresh. The trade-off: a write that fails to invalidate (because the cache `DEL` call fails) leaves stale data until TTL expires, so cache-aside requires either a reliable invalidation path or a bounded TTL as a safety net.

The headline **race conditions** of cache-aside are well-known and must be designed around. The **"cache miss, DB read, cache set" window**: between the miss and the set, a concurrent write may update the DB and invalidate (or set) the cache — and then the original reader's set overwrites with stale data. Mitigation: use `SETNX` (set-if-not-exists) or a short TTL so the staleness window is bounded. The **"stale-then-overwrite" race**: a write updates the DB and deletes the cache; simultaneously, a read that started before the write fetches the old value from the DB and writes it back to the cache — restoring stale data. Mitigation: delayed double-delete (delete, sleep 100 ms, delete again) or use a write-through pattern instead. The **"thundering herd"**: a popular key expires and thousands of concurrent reads all miss, all query the DB, all set the cache. Mitigation: per-key locking (only the first miss fetches; others wait), or probabilistic early expiration. Each of these races is rare but real; Netflix and Uber have published post-mortems of outages caused by exactly these patterns.

The **advantages** of cache-aside are clear: the cache is a pure optimization — if it disappears, the application still works (just slower); the cache can be rebuilt at any time by warming it; TTLs and eviction are explicit and per-key; and the cache layer (Redis/memcached) needs no knowledge of the database schema. The **disadvantages** are equally clear: application code is more complex (every read has miss-handling); race conditions are possible and must be designed around; the cache can serve stale data between a write and the next invalidation; and there is no built-in consistency guarantee. For workloads where these disadvantages matter — strong consistency, frequent writes, complex miss-handling — read-through, write-through, or write-behind patterns are better fits. Cache-aside is the right default for read-heavy workloads with eventual-consistency tolerance: user profiles, product catalogs, recommendation rows, social-graph snapshots.

A subtle but important cache-aside decision is **what to use as the cache key**. The key must uniquely identify the cached value, include any relevant dimensions (user id, locale, version), and be deterministic given the same input. Netflix uses keys like `profile:{user_id}:v3` for the profile (the `v3` suffix lets them change the cache format without invalidating old keys — just bump the version and old keys naturally expire by TTL). Instagram uses `feed:{user_id}:page_{n}` for paginated feeds. Amazon uses `product:{asin}:locale_{lang}` so the same product in different locales caches separately. Choosing keys well is half the battle — bad keys cause collisions, unnecessary misses, or stale data served to the wrong user.

Finally, cache-aside scales gracefully because the cache itself is stateless from the application's perspective. Adding more Redis shards distributes the load; losing a shard just causes more misses (the application falls through to the DB); warming a fresh cache is a matter of replaying reads. This is why Netflix can run chaos experiments that kill cache nodes — the system degrades gracefully to "more DB load, higher latency" rather than failing outright. The cache is a performance optimization, not a correctness-critical component, and that property is what makes cache-aside the safest first choice when introducing caching to a new service.

WHERE key=? DB-->>App: row App->>Cache: SET key value TTL (back-fill) Cache-->>App: OK end App-->>App: return value Note over App,DB: WRITE PATH (invalidate variant) App->>DB: UPDATE ... WHERE key=? DB-->>App: rows affected App->>Cache: DEL key Cache-->>App: OK Note right of Cache: next read will miss,
fetch fresh from DB,
and repopulate ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` READ PATH (cache-aside): +----------+ GET key +----------+ | App |------------>| Cache | +----------+ +----------+ | | | | hit? yes |<----------------------+ | return value | (done, sub-millisecond) | | miss v +----------+ SELECT +----------+ | App |----------->| DB | +----------+ +----------+ | | SET key value TTL (back-fill) v +----------+ | Cache | +----------+ | | return value WRITE PATH (invalidate): +----------+ UPDATE +----------+ | App |----------->| DB | +----------+ +----------+ | | DEL key (invalidate, NOT set) v +----------+ | Cache | +----------+ | | next read will miss, | fetch fresh, repopulate v ... ``` ### Walkthrough 1. **Read**: The application calls `cache.get(key)`. If the cache returns a value (hit), the request completes in under a millisecond — no DB call, no deserialization, no compute. 2. **Miss handling**: On a miss, the application queries the database (typically a few milliseconds), then writes the result back to the cache with a TTL (`cache.set(key, value, ttl)`) so subsequent reads hit the cache. 3. **Write**: When the application updates the data, it writes to the database first (source of truth), then invalidates the cache entry (`cache.del(key)`). The next read misses, re-fetches the fresh value from the DB, and repopulates the cache. The cache is never authoritative — the DB is, and the cache is a performance-optimizing shadow.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- A minimal cache-aside implementation.
- Read path: cache first, miss -> DB -> back-fill cache.
- Back-fill / explicit set.
- Write path: delete cache entry, next read will re-fetch from DB.
- Cache-Aside pattern: application explicitly manages cache (get/set/del).
- Demonstrates read miss-handling and write-invalidate, plus a stampede guard.
- Miss: acquire per-key lock to prevent stampede.
- Double-check after acquiring lock (another thread may have filled).

**Defines:** `CacheAside`, `fake_db_loader()`, `fake_db_writer()`

```python
# Cache-Aside pattern: application explicitly manages cache (get/set/del).
# Demonstrates read miss-handling and write-invalidate, plus a stampede guard.

import threading
import time
import random
from typing import Callable, Optional, Dict, Any

class CacheAside:
    """A minimal cache-aside implementation.

    The application owns the read-miss and write-invalidate logic.
    The cache is a dumb key-value store; the DB is the source of truth.
    """

    def __init__(self, db_loader: Callable[[str], Any], ttl_seconds: int = 60):
        self._cache: Dict[str, tuple] = {}            # key -> (value, expires_at)
        self._db_loader = db_loader
        self._ttl = ttl_seconds
        self._locks: Dict[str, threading.Lock] = {}   # per-key stampede guard
        self._lock_mu = threading.Lock()
        self.stats = {"hits": 0, "misses": 0, "sets": 0, "deletes": 0}

    def _get_lock(self, key: str) -> threading.Lock:
        with self._lock_mu:
            if key not in self._locks:
                self._locks[key] = threading.Lock()
            return self._locks[key]

    def get(self, key: str) -> Any:
        """Read path: cache first, miss -> DB -> back-fill cache."""
        entry = self._cache.get(key)
        if entry and entry[1] > time.time():
            self.stats["hits"] += 1
            return entry[0]
        # Miss: acquire per-key lock to prevent stampede.
        with self._get_lock(key):
            # Double-check after acquiring lock (another thread may have filled).
            entry = self._cache.get(key)
            if entry and entry[1] > time.time():
                self.stats["hits"] += 1
                return entry[0]
            self.stats["misses"] += 1
            value = self._db_loader(key)              # fall through to DB
            self.set(key, value)                      # back-fill cache
            return value

    def set(self, key: str, value: Any) -> None:
        """Back-fill / explicit set."""
        self._cache[key] = (value, time.time() + self._ttl)
        self.stats["sets"] += 1

    def invalidate(self, key: str) -> None:
        """Write path: delete cache entry, next read will re-fetch from DB."""
        self._cache.pop(key, None)
        self.stats["deletes"] += 1

    # The application typically wraps writes like this:
    def write_through_db(self, key: str, new_value: Any,
                         db_writer: Callable[[str, Any], None]) -> None:
        db_writer(key, new_value)                     # update source of truth
        self.invalidate(key)                          # invalidate cache

# ---------- Demo ---------- #
def fake_db_loader(key: str) -> str:
    """Simulate a slow DB read."""
    time.sleep(0.05)  # 50 ms
    return f"value_for_{key}_at_{int(time.time())}"

def fake_db_writer(key: str, value: str) -> None:
    """Simulate a DB write."""
    time.sleep(0.02)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cache = CacheAside(fake_db_loader, ttl_seconds=5)

    print("--- First read (miss, hits DB, back-fills cache) ---")
    t0 = time.time()
    v1 = cache.get("user:42")
    print(f"  value={v1}  latency={ (time.time()-t0)*1000:.0f} ms")

    print("\n--- Second read (hit, no DB call) ---")
    t0 = time.time()
    v2 = cache.get("user:42")
    print(f"  value={v2}  latency={ (time.time()-t0)*1000:.0f} ms")

    print("\n--- Write (updates DB, invalidates cache) ---")
    cache.write_through_db("user:42", "updated_value", fake_db_writer)

    print("\n--- Read after write (miss, fetches fresh value) ---")
    t0 = time.time()
    v3 = cache.get("user:42")
    print(f"  value={v3}  latency={ (time.time()-t0)*1000:.0f} ms")

    print("\n--- Stampede test: 50 concurrent reads on cold key ---")
    cache.invalidate("hot:key")
    results = []
    def worker():
        t = time.time()
        cache.get("hot:key")
        results.append(time.time() - t)
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(50)]
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()
    print(f"  50 threads, max latency={max(results)*1000:.0f} ms "
          f"(stampede guard -> only 1 DB call, others waited)")
    print(f"\n  Stats: {cache.stats}")
```

The cache is a "dumb" key-value store — it has no knowledge of the DB schema, no loader, no automatic behavior.

quiz.explanation: In most production systems, invalidate (DEL) is preferred over update (SET). Reasons: (1) Invalidation is idempotent — DEL twice has the same effect as DEL once, while SET with different values races on last-writer-wins. (2) Invalidation avoids computing the new cache value if no one reads it soon — a write-only key never incurs the cache-set cost.
